params.title: MF-HF-DSC-SITOR (NBDP) Equip. & Ops
params.subtitle: The ship's long-range radio: its frequencies and signals, how its receiver and transmitter work, and how to find their faults.

scenes.narration: Welcome to the second lesson of Element 9. Every ship in the GMDSS, the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System, carries a long-range radio station for the medium frequency and high frequency bands, MF and HF for short. With it, the ship can send a distress alert, talk by voice and exchange typed messages. As its maintainer, you're the one who keeps it working. By the end of this lesson you'll know the frequencies it uses, what its controls do, how its signals are made and received, and how to track down a fault from the symptoms and meter readings. No electronics background is needed: we'll build each idea from the ground up.

params.title: Refresher: frequency and the radio bands

onScreen: Frequency: cycles each second, in hertz
scenes.narration: First, a quick refresher. A radio wave is energy that swings back and forth, over and over, as it travels. One complete swing is a cycle, and the number of cycles every second is the frequency, measured in hertz. 1 hertz is 1 cycle each second. A kilohertz is 1000 hertz, and a megahertz is 1000 kilohertz. Radio frequencies are grouped into bands. Medium frequency, MF, runs from 300 kilohertz to 3 megahertz. High frequency, HF, runs from 3 to 30 megahertz. Above that is very high frequency, VHF, used by short-range ship radios. One more idea we'll need later: the lower the frequency, the longer each wave is from crest to crest.

params.title: How MF, HF and VHF travel

onScreen: MF ground wave: about 100 to 150 nm by day
scenes.narration: Why does a ship need MF and HF? It's about reach. On the 2 megahertz MF band, the wave follows the curve of the sea as a ground wave. By day it normally reaches roughly 100 to 150 nautical miles; a nautical mile is a little longer than a land mile. HF waves bounce off the ionosphere, a layer of electrically charged gas high in the atmosphere, and come down far away, even across an ocean. Which HF band works best depends on distance and time of day, so there are several. VHF, by contrast, reaches only to about the horizon.

params.title: A first fault check: 2182 kHz by day

marks.label: 60 miles
marks.note: No contact by day: a malfunction

onScreen: 60 miles, no contact by day: malfunction
Ground wave by day: about 100 to 150 nm
600 nm, no contact by day: normal
scenes.narration: That reach gives you a first fault check. 2182 kilohertz is the ship's main MF voice frequency, in the 2 megahertz band, so it travels by ground wave. Suppose that by day you fail to contact another station only 60 miles away. That indicates a malfunction of the 2182 kilohertz radiotelephone system, the ship's MF voice radio, because 60 miles is well inside the 100 to 150 nautical miles a daytime ground wave normally covers. But failing to reach a shore station 600 nautical miles away by day is normal. That's far beyond ground-wave range, so it's no sign of trouble.

params.title: Step 1: a DSC call
items: DSC, digital selective calling: a short digital call
It rings only the station you choose, and shows who is calling and why
A distress alert: a DSC call to all stations
Each ship is known by its MMSI, a 9-digit number

onScreen: Distress alert: a call to all stations
scenes.narration: So that's how far the station reaches. What does it do with that reach? Every contact works in 2 steps: first a call, then the conversation. The call is made by DSC, digital selective calling. It's a short digital message, a bit like a phone call that rings only the station you choose and shows who is calling and why. A distress alert is a DSC call to all stations at once. DSC knows each ship by its MMSI, Maritime Mobile Service Identity: a 9 digit number that works like the ship's phone number.

params.title: Step 2: talk on a follow-on frequency

blocks.label: Follow-on frequency
blocks.note: Same band: where the conversation happens

blocks.label: SITOR (NBDP) radio telex
blocks.note: Typed text, printed at the far end

onScreen: Both stations move to a follow-on frequency
scenes.narration: Once the call gets through, both stations move off the DSC frequency to a follow-on frequency in the same band. That keeps the DSC frequency clear for the next alert. The conversation happens on the follow-on frequency, in one of 2 ways. The stations can talk by voice, using the radio like a telephone. Or they can exchange typed messages by radio telex. Radio telex on MF and HF is SITOR, simplex teletype over radio: the stations take turns sending, and the text prints out at the far end. It's also called NBDP, narrow-band direct printing.

params.title: DSC and follow-on frequencies, band by band

onScreen: DSC is the highest of the 3 in every band
scenes.narration: So where do the calls and conversations happen? Each band, from 2 to 16 megahertz, has 3 frequencies to know, all in kilohertz: one for DSC, one for voice follow-on and one for SITOR, or NBDP, follow-on. Watch for a pattern as we read across: DSC is always the highest of the 3. In the 2 megahertz band, DSC is 2187.5, voice 2182 and NBDP 2174.5. In the 4 megahertz band, 4207.5, 4125 and 4177.5. From here up, voice is the lowest; only at 2 megahertz does NBDP sit below it. At 6 megahertz: 6312, 6215 and 6268. At 8 megahertz: 8414.5, 8291 and 8376.5. Then 12577, 12290 and 12520 at 12 megahertz, and 16804.5, 16420 and 16695 at 16.

params.title: Spotting the trap answers
items: Exam voice set: 4125, 8291 and 16420 kHz
Exam SITOR (NBDP) set: 2174.5, 6268 and 12520 kHz
6312 and 8414.5 kHz are DSC, never follow-on
2182, 4125, 4177.5, 8291, 8376.5 and 12520 kHz are follow-on, never DSC

scenes.narration: On the exam, each use is asked as a set, and the wrong choices slip in a frequency from another list. The correct DSC set is 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kilohertz. For follow-on, the exam's answer pairs a voice set of 4125, 8291 and 16420 kilohertz with an NBDP set of 2174.5, 6268 and 12520. So watch for strangers. DSC frequencies such as 6312 and 8414.5 are not follow-on channels. And follow-on frequencies such as 2182, 4125, 4177.5, 8291, 8376.5 and 12520 are not DSC frequencies: if a DSC answer contains any of them, it's wrong.

params.title: How a voice rides on a radio wave
labels: Carrier: a steady wave at the channel frequency
Modulation: the voice changes the carrier
Sidebands: new frequencies just above and below
AM, A3E: carrier plus 2 mirror-image sidebands

onScreen: Carrier: a steady wave, no information
scenes.narration: Those are the channels. Now, how does a voice travel on one? The transmitter makes a steady radio wave on the channel frequency, called the carrier. On its own, a carrier holds no information, like a steady hum. Modulation means changing the carrier in step with the voice. In ordinary AM, amplitude modulation, the voice makes the carrier's amplitude, its strength, rise and fall. That creates new frequencies just above and below the carrier, called sidebands. Each holds a complete copy of the voice, one a mirror image of the other. In this picture, frequency runs from left to right: the carrier in the middle, a sideband on each side. Each kind of signal has a short label, its emission code, and this one, full-carrier AM with both sidebands, is A3E.

params.title: Single sideband: J3E
labels: Carrier removed: it carries no voice
Lower sideband removed: it's a duplicate
J3E: one sideband, carrier suppressed
The receiver must put a carrier back

onScreen: The receiver must restore the carrier
scenes.narration: That's AM, and it wastes power. The carrier takes most of it yet carries no voice, and the 2 sidebands are duplicates. So marine voice uses single sideband, or SSB. The transmitter suppresses the carrier and sends just one sideband, the upper one. All the power goes into the voice, and the signal takes half the room. That's emission J3E. There's a catch. The sideband is the voice moved up to radio frequency. To move it back down to sound, the receiver needs a carrier exactly where the missing one was, so it makes its own and adds it back. If that home-made carrier is slightly off, every voice comes out too high or too low and sounds garbled. Remember that: it explains several faults later.

params.title: Bandwidth and channel spacing
items: Bandwidth: how wide a slice of frequencies a signal fills
Channel spacing: the distance from one channel to the next
J3E voice: 2.8 kHz assigned bandwidth, the 2K80J3E emission
J3E channel spacing: 3.0 kHz, a little wider than the signal

onScreen: Bandwidth: the width a signal fills
scenes.narration: So how much room does a voice take? A voice signal isn't a single frequency: its sideband spreads over a range of frequencies, and the width of that range is the bandwidth. Think of the band as a highway. The bandwidth is how wide your vehicle is, and the channel spacing is how far apart the lanes are. An SSB voice signal, J3E, has an assigned bandwidth of 2.8 kilohertz, enough for the pitches that make speech clear. That's why its full emission code is written 2 K 80 J 3 E: the 2 K 80 in front gives the bandwidth, 2.8 kilohertz, with the K standing in for the decimal point. Voice channels are spaced 3.0 kilohertz apart, a little wider than the signal, so neighbors don't overlap.

params.title: Digital signals: frequency-shift keying
labels: Digital: information as 1s and 0s, called bits
FSK: one frequency means 1, another means 0
DSC and SITOR (NBDP): a 170 Hz shift
100 baud: 100 bits each second

scenes.narration: Voice is one kind of signal. DSC and radio telex are digital: they send information as a string of 1s and 0s, called bits. To send bits by radio, the transmitter uses frequency-shift keying, or FSK; keying is an old telegraph word for switching. It switches between 2 frequencies: one means 1, the other means 0. On MF and HF, DSC and SITOR, or NBDP, both use 2 frequencies just 170 hertz apart, called a 170 hertz shift. The speed is measured in baud, the number of signal changes each second. Here 1 change carries 1 bit, so 100 baud means 100 bits every second.

params.title: Telex versus voice: bandwidth and spacing

onScreen: J2B SITOR (NBDP): 300 Hz bandwidth, 500 Hz spacing
170 Hz shift at 100 baud fits in about 300 Hz
J3E voice: 2.8 kHz bandwidth, 3.0 kHz spacing
scenes.narration: How much room does telex need? Far less than voice. SITOR, or NBDP, sent through the SSB transmitter, has the emission code J2B. Its assigned bandwidth is only 300 hertz, and its channels are spaced 500 hertz apart. Why so narrow? The 2 FSK frequencies are only 170 hertz apart, and at a slow 100 baud the signal spreads only a little beyond them, so it all fits in about 300 hertz. Compare voice: 2.8 kilohertz of bandwidth on channels 3.0 kilohertz apart. The wrong answers swap the 2 pairs, so tie each pair to its signal: voice is the wide one, telex the narrow one.

params.title: Reading emission codes
rows: A: carrier keyed on and off

onScreen: First letter: carrier · number: signal · last letter: use
scenes.narration: You've met a few emission codes now. Each has 3 parts: the first letter says how the carrier is modulated, the number says what kind of signal it carries, and the last letter says what it's for. Take A3E: the letter A means AM with both sidebands, 3 means an analog signal such as voice, and E means voice, or telephony. H3E is voice too, but H means single sideband with the full carrier kept. In J3E, J means single sideband with the carrier suppressed. J2B and F1B are telex. In J2B, the 2 means digital keying carried on an audio tone; in F1B, the F means the frequency itself shifts, and the 1 means direct keying. Both end in B: telegraphy printed by machine. Last, A1A is Morse code: a carrier keyed on and off, copied by ear.

onScreen: Tolerance: how far off frequency is allowed
Keeps 170 Hz-shift signals in narrow filters
scenes.narration: Whatever the code, every signal has to sit on its channel. But no transmitter stays exactly on its assigned frequency: it drifts a little. Frequency tolerance is the most it's allowed to be off. For GMDSS MF-HF transmitters, the allowable frequency tolerance is 10 hertz, up or down. That's tiny: 10 hertz out of millions, like keeping a car in the middle of a very narrow lane. Why so tight? DSC and NBDP signals shift only 170 hertz, and the receiver catches them with narrow filters, circuits that let through only a thin slice of frequencies. Even a small error could push a signal off target. It also keeps SSB voices at their natural pitch.

params.title: Is it within tolerance?
steps: Other pairs: 9 or 10 Hz off, at or near the limit
Flag: a 2 ppm counter can be off ≈4.4 or 8.3 Hz

scenes.narration: The exam turns this into a worked example. You measure transmitters on 2182 and 4125 kilohertz with a frequency counter accurate to 2 parts per million: its own error can be up to 2 hertz for every million hertz it measures. Which pair of readings is within tolerance? Subtract the assigned frequency from each reading. Since a kilohertz is 1000 hertz, the 3 digits after the decimal point count hertz. 2182.006 is 6 hertz high. 4124.995 is 5 hertz low. Every other answer pair includes an offset of 9 or 10 hertz, at or near the limit. A flag note: 2 parts per million of 2182 kilohertz is about 4.4 hertz, and of 4125 about 8.3 hertz, so the counter itself could be that far off. For the exam, choose 2182.006 and 4124.995 kilohertz, the smallest offsets.

That completes the band plan and the signals. Now let's open up the DSC call that starts every contact, beginning with how its bits are sent. On MF and HF, the DSC signal is made from 2 audio tones fed into the SSB transmitter, which moves them up to radio frequency just as it does a voice. The tones are built around a 1700 hertz sub-carrier, an audio center tone that carries the data inside the radio signal, shifted plus or minus 85 hertz. That gives 1615 hertz and 1785 hertz, 170 hertz apart: the 170 hertz shift. They alternate at 100 baud. So for MF-HF DSC, the frequency shift is plus or minus 85 hertz, and the sub-carrier is 1700 hertz.

params.title: Anatomy of a DSC distress alert

badges.label: Dot pattern: alternating 1s and 0s
badges.note: Scanning receivers stop and lock onto the timing

badges.label: The message
badges.note: The call itself, character by character

scenes.narration: Those tones carry the bits. Next, the order they come in: a DSC distress alert has a fixed layout. A ship's DSC watch receiver doesn't sit on one frequency: it scans, hopping between DSC frequencies, listening for a call. So every call starts with a wake-up signal: an alternating dot pattern of 1s and 0s, 200 bits long. At 100 baud, 200 bits last 2 seconds, long enough for a scanning receiver to stop on the frequency and lock onto the bit timing. That locking is called synchronizing. The dot pattern precedes the phasing signal, which tells the receiver where each character begins. Then comes the message itself, character by character.

params.title: Each DSC character: a 10-bit code
rows: A count of the 0 bits in the 7

onScreen: 3 error-check bits: a count of the 0s
Not DSC: a 7-bit code with a 4/3 ratio
scenes.narration: Inside the message, each DSC character is a 10 bit code, in 2 parts. 7 bits carry the information, the character itself. The other 3 bits are for error checking: they hold a count of how many 0 bits are in the information part. On arrival, the receiver counts the 0s itself and compares. If the counts don't match, a bit was damaged on the way, and the receiver knows that copy is bad. That's why the exam says 7 bits for information and 3 for error correction. The trap answer is a 7 bit code with a constant 4 to 3 ratio of 1s to 0s. That's SITOR's code, which we'll meet shortly, not DSC's.

So what happens to a bad copy? DSC sends every character twice, at 2 different times. This is called time diversity: a burst of static that wipes out one copy will probably miss the other. On MF and HF, 4 other characters are sent between the first copy of a character and its repeat. Let's work out that gap. 4 characters times 10 bits each is 40 bits. At 100 bits per second, 100 bits take 1 second, so 40 bits take 4 tenths of a second: 400 milliseconds. A millisecond is a thousandth of a second. So the MF-HF DSC time diversity reception interval is 400 milliseconds, a number the exam tests.

Ships also use DSC on VHF, and the exam likes to mix the 2 up, so compare them feature by feature. The tones: MF-HF DSC uses 1615 and 1785 hertz, which is 1700 plus or minus 85 hertz, while VHF DSC uses 1300 and 2100 hertz. The speed: MF-HF sends at a slow 100 baud, VHF at 1200 baud. Why so slow on MF and HF? Long-distance signals fade and crackle with static, and a slow, narrow signal survives that better. And the time diversity interval: 400 milliseconds on MF-HF, but only 33 and a third milliseconds on VHF. So if you see 1300 and 2100 hertz, that's VHF, not MF-HF.

params.title: What a distress alert carries
items: The ship's MMSI: its 9-digit identity
Its position
The nature of distress, such as fire or sinking
Follow-on communications: J3E voice or F1B telex
Ships are identified by MMSI, not by call sign or vessel name

onScreen: MMSI, not call sign or name
scenes.narration: Now, what a distress alert actually says. Distress is the highest priority a DSC call can have. An MF-HF distress priority DSC call may include the ship's MMSI, its position, the nature of distress, such as fire or sinking, and how follow-on communications will be made: by J3E voice or F1B telex. Notice what's not on the list: no call sign and no vessel name. DSC identifies ships by MMSI. So the trap answers that swap in the call sign or the vessel name are wrong, and so is the one that says J3E only, since F1B telex is allowed too.

callouts.label: 003669999: group call for all U.S. Coast Guard coast stations
Received by all DSC-equipped USCG coast stations in range
They may send an automated acknowledgement
True: it may be used to test ship MF-HF DSC equipment

onScreen: Received by all DSC-equipped USCG coast stations in range
May be used to test ship MF-HF DSC
scenes.narration: One MMSI to know by heart: 0 0 3 6 6 9 9 9 9. It's a group call, an MMSI that addresses many stations at once: all U.S. Coast Guard coast stations. A DSC call to it is received by all DSC-equipped Coast Guard coast stations within radio range, and they may send back an automated acknowledgement. That makes it handy for checking your own equipment: calls to 0 0 3 6 6 9 9 9 9 may be used to test MF-HF DSC equipment aboard ships. The exam asks which statement is false, and the false one says these calls may not be used for testing.

params.title: SITOR (NBDP): 3 ways to send
rows: A station that must not transmit

onScreen: SFEC: one-way, to a single station
scenes.narration: DSC sets up a contact. For longer messages, ships use SITOR radio telex. Radio paths are noisy, so SITOR has 2 ways of fighting errors, used in 3 modes. ARQ, automatic repeat request, is two-way: the receiving station checks each piece and asks for a repeat when something's wrong. FEC, forward error correction, is one-way to all stations: it sends everything twice, so no reply is needed. SFEC, selective FEC, is one-way to a single station. It's used when one particular station must receive messages without transmitting, such as a ship keeping radio silence: one station, not many, and it never transmits, not even to get in step. So the sequence ARQ, FEC, SFEC means: two-way, one-way to all stations, one-way to a single station.

params.title: The SITOR code: checking built in
items: Each SITOR character: 7 bits
Always exactly 4 ones and 3 zeros: a fixed 4:3 ratio
A flipped bit breaks the ratio
Checking the ratio is the parity check

onScreen: A flipped bit breaks the ratio
scenes.narration: ARQ's checking relies on SITOR's code. Each character is 7 bits long, and every valid character has exactly 4 ones and 3 zeros: a fixed 4 to 3 ratio. If static flips a bit, turning a 1 into a 0 or a 0 into a 1, the count is no longer 4 and 3, so the receiver can tell the character is damaged. Checking that ratio is what the exam calls the parity check. Remember, this 7 bit, 4 to 3 code is SITOR's. DSC uses the 10 bit code with 3 check bits.

badges.label: Block correct
badges.note: The ISS sends the next 3 characters

badges.label: Parity check fails
badges.note: The IRS asks for the same block again

onScreen: ISS sends a block of 3 characters
scenes.narration: Here's an ARQ exchange. The sending station is the ISS, the information sending station. It transmits a block of 3 characters, then stops and listens. The receiving station is the IRS, the information receiving station. It checks the block for parity, the 4 to 3 ratio. If the block is correct, it sends a short control signal telling the ISS to proceed. If the parity check fails, the block must be resent. When a ship works a shore station, it goes like this: the ship sends a group of 3 characters, and the shore station checks parity. If parity is OK, the shore station indicates readiness for the next 3 characters; it asks for a repeat only when the check fails.

onScreen: Not ARQ: each character sent twice
Broadcasts can't be copied in ARQ
scenes.narration: ARQ has a steady rhythm. The ISS sends a block of 3 characters lasting 210 milliseconds, then pauses to listen for the reply, and the whole cycle repeats every 450 milliseconds. Remember that rhythm: we'll see it again on the transmitter's power meter. Because ARQ needs a reply after every block, it only works between 2 stations that both transmit. That rules out 2 trap answers. Sending each character twice belongs to FEC, not ARQ. And broadcasts are one-way: NAVTEX, the coastal service that broadcasts maritime safety information, or MSI, such as navigation and weather warnings, can't be contacted, and its broadcasts can't be copied in ARQ.

params.title: Working an automated coast station
items: Most ARQ commands end with '+', as in HELP+ and MSG+
HELP+: ask for help with the commands
MSG+: retrieve messages waiting for you
AMV+: send an AMVER report
OPR+: call the coast station operator

scenes.narration: ARQ is how a ship works a coast station, and many coast stations are automated: a computer answers in ARQ and takes typed commands. When working an automated coast station, most ARQ commands are followed by a plus sign, which works like pressing Enter: the station acts once it arrives. HELP plus asks for help with the commands. M S G plus retrieves messages waiting for you. A M V plus sends an AMVER report, to the Automated Mutual-assistance Vessel Rescue system, which keeps track of ships so rescuers can find nearby help. O P R plus calls the station's human operator. On the exam, the character that follows most commands is the plus sign, not ENTER and not END.

params.title: Direct telex to a shore subscriber

onScreen: Coast station joins radio and land line
KKKK ends the direct TELEX connection
scenes.narration: One command needs a closer look. A TELEX subscriber is an office ashore with its own number on the land-line telex network. To send a message via a direct connection to a shoreside TELEX subscriber, the ship sends D I R T L X, the subscriber's telex number, and a plus sign. The exam writes the number part as 0, x x, y y y y. The coast station then joins the radio circuit to the subscriber's land line, and the 2 ends exchange text directly. When you're done, send K K K K. That terminates the direct TELEX connection, clearing the land-line link, while the radio circuit can stay up for more commands. The trap answers are END plus and E O M, end of message.

params.title: FEC: every character sent twice
labels: Mode B, FEC: each character sent twice, separated in time
A static crash corrupts one copy
The receiver uses the other copy
No reply needed: one-way

onScreen: Mode B FEC: each character sent twice
A static crash corrupts a copy
scenes.narration: That's ARQ. FEC, also called SITOR Mode B, takes the other approach. It can't ask for a repeat, because nobody replies. Instead, it transmits each character twice, separated in time, far enough apart that one burst of noise rarely hits both. A static crash is a short burst of noise, often from distant lightning. If one wipes out a copy of a character, as it does here, the receiver uses the other copy. So FEC reduces the error rate in the presence of static crashes by transmitting each character twice. The cost is time, since everything goes out twice. The benefit is that any number of stations can copy it without transmitting a thing.

params.title: NAVTEX and Sat-C down? Use the console

onScreen: NAVTEX receiver and Sat-C both down
Not ARQ: it can't copy a broadcast
scenes.narration: FEC is how safety broadcasts reach ships. Remember MSI: navigation warnings, weather forecasts and other urgent safety news. Near the coast it comes by NAVTEX: broadcasts on 518 kilohertz, sent in FEC and printed by a dedicated NAVTEX receiver. It also arrives by satellite on the Inmarsat-C terminal, Sat-C for short. Now suppose you're within range of NAVTEX broadcasts, but both the Inmarsat-C and the NAVTEX receiver are inoperative. The MF-HF console can stand in: that's the ship's MF-HF transceiver, its combined transmitter and receiver. Select 518 kilohertz FEC TELEX on the MF-HF console to receive MSI. Not ARQ: ARQ needs a two-way link, and it can't copy a broadcast.

params.title: Beyond NAVTEX: the HF MSI frequencies

marks.label: 4210 kHz
marks.note: Lowest of the 8 HF MSI frequencies

onScreen: Beyond NAVTEX range, Sat-C failed: HF MSI frequency, FEC TELEX
Tropical static spoiling NAVTEX: same fix
scenes.narration: What if you're beyond range of NAVTEX broadcasts and the Sat-C system fails? MSI is also broadcast on HF, which reaches far out to sea. Select an HF MSI frequency and FEC TELEX mode to receive MSI. The same fix works when atmospheric interference spoils NAVTEX, especially in the tropics, where thunderstorm static is heavy on MF. Select one of the 8 HF MSI frequencies, which run from 4210 to 26100.5 kilohertz, and set up the transceiver in FEC TELEX mode. The wrong answers offer ARQ, 6 frequencies, or MF ones. Remember: 8 HF frequencies, and always FEC for a broadcast.

params.title: At the console: display and keypad

callouts.label: TLX on the display: operating in SITOR (NBDP)
ENTER: accepts the previous selection or data input
Distress alert: a separate, covered button

scenes.narration: You've now seen the signals and modes this station uses. Let's sit down at the MF-HF transceiver itself. Its display shows the mode. When it shows TLX, short for telex, the transceiver is operating in SITOR, or NBDP. The keypad is how you enter things such as a frequency or an MMSI. The ENTER function accepts the previous selection or data input, the way Enter does on a computer. It doesn't send a distress alert: that has its own separate, covered button, so it can't be pressed by accident. The other knobs and buttons make sense once you know the circuits behind them, so we'll meet each one there.

callouts.label: Whip antenna: sends and picks up the radio waves
Antenna coupler, or tuner: matches antenna and radio
Coax transmission line down to the radio

scenes.narration: Both the receiver and the transmitter meet the outside world at the antenna, so let's start there. A ship's MF-HF antenna is usually a tall whip, a single upright rod. On transmit, it turns the radio's power into radio waves; on receive, it picks the waves up. At its base sits the antenna coupler, also called the antenna tuner, a box that matches the antenna to the radio. From the coupler, a transmission line carries the signal down to the radio. That line is coaxial cable, or coax: a center wire inside a tube-shaped shield, with insulation between them.

params.title: Resonance and wavelength
labels: Resonance: the antenna's natural frequency
Wavelength: from one crest to the next
At 2 MHz, one wave is about 150 meters long
A ship's whip is far too short for MF on its own

onScreen: The whip is too short for MF
scenes.narration: Why does the antenna need a tuner at all? An antenna works best at its resonant frequency, its natural frequency, like a swing that goes highest when you push it in time with its natural rhythm. That natural frequency depends on the antenna's length compared with the wavelength, the distance from one wave crest to the next. Lower frequencies have longer waves: at 2 megahertz, one wavelength is about 150 meters. A ship's whip is far shorter than that, so on MF it's much too short to be resonant by itself. And the station works on many frequencies, while the whip has just one natural frequency. Something has to make up the difference on every channel.

params.title: Refresher: current, voltage and resistance
items: Current: a flow of electric charge, like water in a pipe
Voltage: the push that drives the current
Resistance: opposition that turns energy into heat, measured in ohms
AC, alternating current: keeps reversing direction, as a radio signal does

scenes.narration: To make up that difference, we need a little electricity. Current is a flow of electric charge along a wire, like water flowing in a pipe. Voltage is the push that drives it, like the water pressure. Anything that holds the flow back opposes it, and the simplest kind of opposition is resistance, which turns energy into heat, the way a heater element warms up. Opposition is measured in ohms. And AC, alternating current, keeps reversing direction, back and forth many times a second, just as a radio signal does.

params.title: Coils, capacitors and reactance
rows: Stores energy in a magnetic field
Stores energy in an electric field

onScreen: Coil: inductive reactance, rises with frequency
Capacitor: capacitive reactance, falls with frequency
A too-short whip acts like a capacitor
scenes.narration: Now 2 parts that behave in a special way with AC. An inductor is a coil of wire; it stores energy in a magnetic field. A capacitor is 2 metal plates with a gap between them; it stores energy in an electric field. With AC, both push back against the flow, but instead of turning energy into heat, they store it and hand it back. That push-back is called reactance, and it's measured in ohms too. A coil's reactance rises as the frequency rises; a capacitor's falls. The 2 kinds push back in opposite ways, so they can cancel each other out. And a whip that's too short behaves like a capacitor.

onScreen: Series inductance: electrically longer, lower resonant frequency
Series capacitance: electrically shorter, higher resonant frequency
scenes.narration: Those 2 parts can change an antenna's electrical length: how long it acts, rather than how long it is. An inductance in series with the antenna electrically lengthens a physically fixed length antenna and lowers its resonant frequency. That's how loading coils let short whips work on MF: the coil cancels the short whip's capacitor-like reactance, so it behaves like a longer antenna. A capacitance in series does the opposite. It electrically shortens a physically fixed length antenna and raises its resonant frequency. The trap answer about increasing bandwidth is wrong for both. Memory hook: coil, longer and lower; capacitor, shorter and higher.

params.title: Impedance, 50 ohms and SWR
items: Impedance: total opposition to AC, resistance plus reactance, in ohms
The MF-HF transmitter and its coax are built for 50 Ω
A mismatch reflects part of the power back down the line
SWR, standing wave ratio: 1:1 is a perfect match; higher means more reflected

scenes.narration: One more idea, and the tuner will make sense. Resistance and reactance together make impedance: the total opposition a circuit offers to AC, in ohms. The MF-HF transmitter is built to feed a 50 ohm load, and its coax is 50 ohm cable. If the antenna also looks like 50 ohms, all the power flows out into it. If not, part of the power reflects back down the cable, like a wave in a rope that hits a wall and bounces back. The forward and reflected waves set up a pattern along the cable called standing waves. The standing wave ratio, or SWR, measures how bad the mismatch is: 1 to 1 is a perfect match, and the higher the number, the more power bounces back.

params.title: The antenna tuner: a match on every frequency

callouts.label: Antenna tuner: matches the antenna to the operating frequency
Cancels the antenna's reactance with coils and capacitors
Transforms the impedance to the transmitter's 50 Ω: SWR minimized

onScreen: Matches the antenna to the operating frequency
scenes.narration: So here's what the tuner does. The purpose of the antenna tuner is to match the antenna to the operating frequency. Inside are coils and capacitors it can switch in and adjust. First, it cancels the antenna's reactance: a too-short whip acts like a capacitor, so the tuner adds inductance to cancel it, just as a loading coil does. Second, it transforms the impedance that's left into the transmitter's 50 ohms. With the antenna looking like a plain 50 ohms, SWR is minimized and full power goes out. Trap answers say it minimizes the carrier, maximizes the sidebands, or provides maximum VSWR. VSWR is another name for SWR, and maximum would be the worst match possible.

onScreen: Antenna matched to 50 Ω at the transmit frequency
scenes.narration: On a GMDSS transceiver the coupler is automatic, and the TUNE button sets it to work. Pressing TUNE tunes the antenna to the transmit frequency. The transmitter usually sends a low-power carrier, a gentle test signal, while the automatic antenna coupler adjusts its matching network, its set of coils and capacitors, until the antenna matches the transmitter's 50 ohm output. Low power protects the transmitter while the match is still poor. Change to a new frequency and the match changes, so it needs tuning again. On the exam, TUNE tunes the antenna, not the receiver, a new channel or the audio amplifier.

onScreen: Not RG-59, RG-6 or RG-179: 72 to 75 Ω
scenes.narration: The cable between radio and coupler has to match too. Every coax has its own impedance, set by its size and construction. RG-8, 50 ohm coax, is suitable for GMDSS MF-HF antenna systems: it matches the 50 ohm transmitter and coupler, and it's thick enough to carry the power. RG-59, RG-6 and RG-179 are 72 to 75 ohm cables, the kind used for TV and video, and they would mismatch the system. At the cable ends, the PL-259 connector is often used in GMDSS MF-HF antenna systems: a sturdy plug with a threaded coupling ring. The others belong elsewhere. F connectors are for 75 ohm TV cable, SMA is a small microwave connector, and EIA-232 is a serial data interface.

params.title: Whip carried away? Rig a wire

blocks.label: 10 ft wire
blocks.note: Too short to tune on MF

onScreen: Rig a 35–40 ft wire per the manual
scenes.narration: Here's a practical problem. A storm breaks off the ship's MF-HF whip antenna and carries it away. How do you get back on the air? Don't connect the VHF antenna: it's built for far higher frequencies and is not usable at MF and HF. A 10 foot wire won't do either: it's too short to tune on MF. Instead, rig a wire antenna approximately 35 to 40 feet long, following the equipment instruction manual. That's roughly the length of the lost whip, so the automatic coupler can match it just as it matched the whip.

blocks.label: I.F. amplifiers and filters
blocks.note: Gain, and only the wanted station

blocks.label: AF amplifier
blocks.note: Squelch mutes it when there's no signal

onScreen: Mixer and oscillator: convert to the I.F.
Detector, with the BFO for SSB
scenes.narration: That's the antenna system. Now follow a signal in through the receiver. It first meets the RF amplifier; RF means radio frequency. Next, the mixer converts it to one fixed frequency, the intermediate frequency, or I.F. The I.F. amplifiers and filters do most of the work: they boost the signal and keep only the station you want. The detector turns it back into audio. 2 oscillators help, each a circuit that makes a steady wave at one frequency. The receiver's own oscillator feeds the mixer and sets which station you hear. The BFO, the beat frequency oscillator, feeds the detector for single sideband. Finally the AF, or audio frequency, amplifier drives the speaker, and its squelch keeps the speaker quiet until a strong enough signal arrives.

params.title: The RF Gain control
items: Amplifier: makes a weak signal stronger; gain is how much
Sensitivity: how weak a signal the receiver can pick up
RF Gain turned down: less sensitivity in the RF amplifier stage
Helps when strong nearby signals or heavy noise overload the receiver

onScreen: Gain: how much an amplifier boosts
RF Gain down: less RF amplifier sensitivity
scenes.narration: The RF amplifier is the first stage you can control. An amplifier makes a weak signal stronger, and its gain is how much stronger. More gain means more sensitivity: the receiver can pick up weaker signals. But more isn't always better. A strong transmitter close by, or heavy noise, can overload a receiver that has too much gain, the way music turned up too loud distorts. Reducing the RF Gain control reduces the sensitivity of the RF amplifier stage. Weak background signals and noise drop away, and the strong signal comes through clean. The trap answers talk about feedback, coupling between stages or volume. RF Gain is about sensitivity.

onScreen: Works through a variable gain amplifier
scenes.narration: RF Gain is set by hand. But signals on MF and HF rise and fade as conditions change, and stations differ hugely in strength. Riding the RF Gain knob all day would be tiring, so the receiver has AGC, automatic gain control. It measures the signal's strength and turns the gain down for strong signals and up for weak ones. It does this by sending a control voltage, a voltage that sets how much an amplifier boosts, to a variable gain amplifier in the RF stage. The result: AGC maintains a relatively constant AF output when the input signal varies. Trap answers get it backwards, such as reducing output when the signal is weak, or raising gain or output when it's strong.

params.title: AGC for SSB voice: fast attack, slow decay

badges.label: Attack: how fast the gain drops
badges.note: Gain cut the instant a voice peak arrives

badges.label: Decay: how fast the gain recovers
badges.note: Held down through gaps, so noise doesn't surge

onScreen: Fast attack: gain drops instantly on peaks
Slow decay: no noise surge between words
scenes.narration: How quickly should AGC react? It has 2 speeds. Attack is how fast it turns the gain down when a strong signal arrives. Decay is how fast it lets the gain back up when the signal drops. SSB voice is tricky, because with no carrier the signal disappears completely between words. An AGC circuit for SSB voice reception should have fast attack and slow decay. Fast attack cuts the gain the instant a voice peak arrives. Slow decay holds it down through the short gaps between words, so background noise doesn't surge up every time the speaker pauses. That's why the other combinations fail: slow attack lets the peaks blast through, and fast decay lets the noise surge.

params.title: The mixer and the intermediate frequency

blocks.label: Receiver's oscillator
blocks.note: Tuned so the difference is the I.F.

onScreen: Fixed I.F.: filters built for one frequency
scenes.narration: Now the stage after the RF amplifier: the mixer. Why convert every station to one intermediate frequency? Because the sharp filters that pick out one station work best when they're built for a single, fixed frequency. So instead of retuning the filters for every channel, the receiver moves each station to the filters. Mixing 2 frequencies produces new ones at their sum and their difference. Mix a 10 megahertz signal with a 12 megahertz wave, and out come 22 megahertz and 2 megahertz. You may have heard 2 nearly equal musical notes make a slow wobble, called a beat: that's a difference frequency too. Tune the oscillator, and you choose which station's difference lands exactly on the I.F. That's the station you hear; everything else misses the I.F. and is filtered out.

marks.label: Receiver's oscillator
marks.note: Example: 12 MHz, 1 I.F. above the wanted

marks.label: Image signal
marks.note: Example: 14 MHz, twice the I.F. away

onScreen: Image: twice the I.F. from the wanted signal
scenes.narration: There's a catch with mixing: the mixer only cares about the difference. Keep the oscillator at 12 megahertz and the I.F. at 2 megahertz. A station at 10 megahertz gives a difference of 2, so it lands on the I.F. But a station at 14 megahertz also gives a difference of 2, so it lands there too, and you'd hear both stations at once. That unwanted station is called an image. It sits on the other side of the oscillator, twice the I.F. away from the wanted signal: 4 megahertz here.

params.title: The cure: a high first I.F.
items: Front end: tuned circuits that pass only frequencies near the wanted one, its passband
Low I.F., like 2 MHz: the image is only 4 MHz away and may slip through
High first I.F.: the image lands far outside the passband and is rejected
Primary purpose of a high first I.F.: eliminating image signals

onScreen: Front end: passes only frequencies near the wanted one
Low I.F.: image close, may slip through
High first I.F.: image far outside the passband
scenes.narration: The cure is to stop the image before it reaches the mixer. The RF stage in front, called the front end, has tuned circuits that pass only frequencies near the wanted one; that range is its passband. With a low I.F. like our 2 megahertz, the image is only 4 megahertz from the wanted signal, close enough that the front end may let it through. Make the first I.F. high, and the image lands far away, well outside the front-end passband, where it's easily rejected. So the primary purpose of a high first I.F. is eliminating image signals.

onScreen: Crystal master oscillator: steady, not tunable
scenes.narration: Now back to the receiver's oscillator. It must be both tunable, to reach any channel, and rock-steady, to stay within a few hertz. No single oscillator does both. A crystal oscillator, built around a slice of quartz that vibrates at one exact rate, is very steady but can't be tuned. In a synthesizer it's called the master oscillator. A voltage controlled oscillator, or VCO, changes frequency when you change its control voltage, so it's easy to tune, but on its own it drifts. The answer is to combine them in a phase locked loop, or PLL. The loop keeps checking the VCO against the crystal and correcting it, like cruise control holding a car's speed. The result is a frequency synthesizer, and the transmitter uses it too.

params.title: Inside the phase locked loop synthesizer

onScreen: Phase comparator: compares the divided outputs
Error voltage pulls the VCO onto frequency
scenes.narration: Here's the loop. Its parts are a master oscillator, frequency dividers, a phase comparator, a loop filter and a voltage controlled oscillator. A frequency divider passes on only 1 cycle out of every so many, dividing the frequency down. Both the master oscillator's output and the VCO's output are divided, and the phase comparator compares the 2 divided outputs. Phase means where a wave is in its cycle, so the comparator checks whether the 2 are in step. If not, it produces an error voltage, which the loop filter smooths and which pulls the VCO onto frequency. To change channels, the radio changes how much the VCO's output is divided. On the exam: the divided outputs of both, never the direct ones, and the wrong parts lists slip in a ratio detector, a mixer or a high pass filter.

onScreen: Low second I.F.: sharp selectivity and gain
scenes.narration: With the oscillator explained, follow the signal on. After the high first I.F., this receiver converts it a second time, down to a low second I.F. Why a second, lower one? At a low frequency it's much easier to build very narrow, sharp filters and to get plenty of gain. Sharpness here is called selectivity: the ability to take one signal and reject its neighbors, even close ones. So the high first I.F. gets rid of images, and the low second I.F. supplies sharp selectivity and gain. Its filters match the signals: voice and SSB go through a 2.8 kilohertz filter, as wide as a voice signal, and SITOR, or NBDP, through a narrow 500 hertz I.F. filter. Remember these 2 paths; they come back in the faults.

params.title: The BFO restores the carrier
labels: J3E arrives with no carrier
The BFO makes a substitute carrier
Re-injected in the detector, it brings the voice back
It does not recreate the missing sideband

scenes.narration: Next, the detector, which turns the signal back into audio; for SSB it's called a product detector. Remember the catch from the start: J3E arrives with its carrier suppressed. Putting a carrier back is the job of the BFO, the beat frequency oscillator, named for the beat, the difference frequency, it makes with the signal. The BFO re-injects the carrier frequency in the receiver's detector to demodulate the SSB signal, which means to recover the voice from it. Mixing the sideband with that substitute carrier brings the voice back down to audio. Note what the BFO does not do: it does not recreate the missing sideband. One sideband is all the voice needs. Trap answers say it replaces the sideband, removes the carrier from H3E, or inverts the signal.

params.title: With the BFO turned off
rows: Still received: has its own carrier
Still received: has its own carrier

onScreen: J2B, F1B, A1A: need the BFO
scenes.narration: So what if the BFO is turned off? Ask which signals bring their own carrier. A3E, double-sideband AM, and H3E, single sideband with full carrier, both transmit a carrier, so they can still be received: a simple detector handles them. J3E has no carrier, so it needs the BFO. So do the telex and Morse signals, J2B, F1B and A1A. Their information is only a shift of frequency or a carrier switching on and off, which a simple detector can't turn into tones; beating them against the BFO does. So with the BFO off, the answer is A3E and H3E.

callouts.label: R.I.T. (clarifier): slight changes to the receive frequency only
Transmit frequency stays on the assigned channel
Garbled voice: adjust R.I.T. until it sounds natural
Not squelch: it only mutes or unmutes the audio

onScreen: R.I.T.: adjusts the receive frequency only
Transmit stays on the assigned channel
scenes.narration: This brings us to a front-panel control. Sometimes one station's voice sounds garbled, too high or too low, like a cartoon duck. Usually your receiver isn't quite on that ship's transmit frequency, so your BFO's carrier doesn't line up with its sideband. The fix is the R.I.T. control, receiver incremental tuning, also called the clarifier. It makes slight adjustments in the receiver frequency only, while your transmit frequency stays on the assigned channel. So if another vessel's HF transmission sounds garbled, use the R.I.T. or Clarifier control to adjust the receiver frequency until the voice sounds natural. Don't reach for squelch: it only mutes or unmutes the audio, and does nothing for sound quality.

blocks.label: Noise pulses
blocks.note: Sharp spikes, such as engine ignition

blocks.label: Noise blanker
blocks.note: Turns each spike into a blanking pulse

blocks.label: I.F. amplifier
blocks.note: Gated off for the length of each spike

onScreen: The I.F. amplifier is gated off briefly
scenes.narration: One more receiver circuit. Some noise comes as sharp, short spikes, such as clicks from an engine's ignition or electrical gear. A noise blanker deals with them. It watches for the noise pulses and uses each one to develop a blanking pulse. The blanking pulse briefly gates off the I.F. amplifier, switching it off for just the length of the spike. The gap is so short you don't notice it, but the click is gone. The trap answers describe other things. Clipping the noise peaks is what a limiter does, a ratio detector belongs to FM receivers, and a blanker doesn't reduce the RF gain.

params.title: Fault finding: shared parts and single paths
items: Every signal fails the same way: suspect a part they all share
Only one mode fails: suspect the part only that mode uses
All SSB voice garbled: the BFO circuit has failed
A failed RF stage or synthesizer: weak or missing signals, not garbled

onScreen: All fail alike: a shared part
One mode fails: its own part
RF stage or synthesizer: weak or missing, not garbled
scenes.narration: That's the whole receiver. Now let's use it to find faults. The trick is to compare what works with what doesn't. If every signal fails the same way, suspect a part they all share. If only one mode fails, suspect a part only that mode uses. Try it. The voice is garbled and unreadable on all the MF-HF SSB channels. Every SSB signal depends on one part to be readable: SSB is understandable only when the BFO reinserts the carrier at the correct frequency. So the most likely cause is a failed beat frequency oscillator circuit. A failed RF stage or synthesizer would leave signals weak or missing, rather than garbled.

params.title: Just one voice sounds wrong
rows: Your BFO, synthesizer and VCO work
That station's transmitter is off frequency

onScreen: One high-pitched voice: that transmitter is off frequency
scenes.narration: Now the opposite case. All signals sound normal except one, which has a very high-pitched voice, barely readable. Use the same logic. If your receiver's BFO, synthesizer or VCO had failed, every station would sound wrong. They all sound fine, so those parts are clearly working. The problem is at the other end: the transmitter of that abnormal signal is off frequency. Its sideband sits away from where your BFO expects it, so the voice comes out pitched up. Your R.I.T. can often compensate.

onScreen: Voice but no NBDP: 500 Hz filter
NBDP but no voice: 2.8 kHz filter
scenes.narration: Next, use the 2 filter paths. Voice and SSB pass through the 2.8 kilohertz filter. SITOR, or NBDP, passes through the narrow 500 hertz I.F. filter. Everything else is shared. Suppose you can hear signals in voice or SSB mode, but not in NBDP mode. The shared stages must be working, because voice gets through them. So suspect the part only NBDP uses: a defective 500 hertz I.F. filter. Now flip it. You hear signals in NBDP mode but not in voice or SSB mode. Then the most likely cause is a defective 2.8 kilohertz filter, the wider path only voice uses.

params.title: Faults inside a circuit
rows: The VCO is part of the loop itself
Failed variable gain amplifier, RF stage
It's the amplifier the AGC controls

onScreen: VCO is part of the loop
AGC inoperative: variable gain amplifier failed
It's what the AGC voltage acts on
scenes.narration: 2 more, and both come from knowing which parts belong to which circuit. If the phase locked loop appears faulty, the most likely cause is an inoperative voltage controlled oscillator. The VCO is part of the loop itself: if it stops oscillating, the phase comparator has nothing to lock, and the whole loop seems dead. The AGC, the BFO and the I.F. filters lie outside the loop. And if the AGC function is inoperative, the most likely cause is failure of a variable gain amplifier in the RF stage. AGC works by sending a control voltage to that amplifier. If the amplifier fails, its gain can't be changed, and the AGC can do nothing.

blocks.label: Dummy load
blocks.note: Connected in place of the antenna

onScreen: Strong AF, no signals: no antenna signal reaches the receiver
Open circuit in the transmission line
Or connected to a dummy load
scenes.narration: Next, the 2 ends of the receiver: the antenna side and the audio side. First clue: the transceiver produces strong AF output, a loud hiss, but no signals are heard on any frequency. The hiss proves the receiver and audio stages work. So no antenna signal is reaching the receiver. There are 2 likely causes. One is an open circuit, a break, in the transmission line to the antenna. The other is that the transceiver is connected to a dummy load. A dummy load is a resistor that stands in for the antenna when testing a transmitter: it soaks up the power as heat without radiating. It picks up nothing either, so the receiver hears only its own noise.

callouts.label: Signal meter swings mid scale to 0: the RF itself comes and goes
Intermittent connection between antenna and coupler
Loose or corroded joints: wind and spray work on them

onScreen: Signal meter swings between mid scale and 0
The meter reads RF, ahead of the audio
scenes.narration: Another clue from the antenna side. A received signal breaks up rapidly and repeatedly, and the Signal meter alternates between mid scale and 0. The Signal meter measures the strength of the incoming RF signal, ahead of the audio stages. So the RF signal itself is coming and going, not just the sound. Something between the antenna and the receiver is making and breaking contact. The most likely cause is an intermittent connection between the antenna and the coupler, the kind of loose or corroded joint that wind and spray work on. A fault in the audio amplifier or the squelch wouldn't move the Signal meter at all.

callouts.label: AF not suppressed with no strong signal: squelch circuit failed
No AF, speaker leads read near 0 Ω: normal for a voice coil
So the audio amplifier stage has failed

onScreen: No AF, speaker near 0 Ω: normal speaker
So the audio amplifier stage failed
scenes.narration: At the other end is the audio side. Suppose the receiver fails to suppress the AF output in the absence of a sufficiently strong input signal. In plain words, the hiss never goes quiet, even with no signal. Muting that hiss is the squelch's whole job, so the squelch circuit has failed. Next, the receiver produces no AF output at all. You check between the speaker leads with an ohmmeter, a meter that measures resistance in ohms, and it reads near 0. Is the speaker shorted? No: a speaker's voice coil, the coil of wire that moves its cone, normally measures only a few ohms, so near 0 is normal. The speaker is fine, and the most likely cause is a failed audio amplifier stage.

params.title: No audio, and TX is lit

onScreen: Shorted Push-To-Talk circuit in the microphone
scenes.narration: One more audio clue, and it's a lamp. The radio is powered on, and TX, the transmit indicator, is illuminated, but there's no AF output. A transceiver mutes its receiver whenever it transmits, so you don't hear yourself. The TX lamp says it's transmitting, though nobody is talking. What tells it to transmit? The push-to-talk button on the microphone. A shorted Push-To-Talk circuit in the microphone holds the set in transmit, which mutes the receiver. Unplug the microphone, and the receiver usually comes back.

onScreen: Second mixer: up to the operating frequency
scenes.narration: That covers the receiver and its faults. Now the transmitter, which runs the receiver's journey in reverse. The microphone's audio, or the telex tones, go first into a balanced mixer, together with a steady carrier from an oscillator. A sideband filter trims the result to a single sideband. These first stages work at one fixed frequency, just like the receiver's I.F. A second mixer, fed by the synthesizer, then moves the signal up to the operating frequency you've chosen. Finally the power amplifier raises it to full power and sends it through the coupler to the antenna. The low-power stages that build the signal are often called the exciter.

onScreen: Double balanced mixer: cancels the carrier
scenes.narration: Let's look closer at how a J3E signal is generated: with a double balanced mixer and a sideband filter. The mixer combines the audio with the carrier oscillator's wave, which creates the 2 sidebands. Balanced means the circuit is built in matched halves that push against each other for the carrier, so the carrier cancels out, like 2 equal teams in a tug of war going nowhere. What comes out is 2 sidebands and no carrier. Then a sharp sideband filter removes one sideband, leaving J3E: single sideband, suppressed carrier. Trap answers mention high-level or low-level modulation, or phase modulating the carrier. The exam's answer is the double balanced mixer and the sideband filter.

onScreen: Marine MF-HF voice uses upper sideband
Lower sideband: blocked by the filter
scenes.narration: Which sideband goes? Marine MF-HF radiotelephony uses the upper sideband, the copy just above the carrier frequency. So the lower sideband is eliminated by a filter that passes the upper sideband and blocks the lower sideband. Watch the trap answers. One has a filter that passes the lower and blocks the upper: backwards. Others give the job to the double balanced mixer. The mixer's job is cancelling the carrier, not choosing a sideband, and it certainly doesn't insert a carrier.

params.title: Peak envelope power: start at 150 W
labels: SSB output rises and falls with the voice
PEP: the power at the highest peaks
Start MF-HF contacts at about 150 watts PEP
Raise it only if the other station can't copy

scenes.narration: That's how the signal is shaped. How strong should it be? First, how SSB power is measured. With no carrier, an SSB transmitter's output rises and falls with the voice: loud syllables make peaks, and pauses make nothing. The outline of those peaks is the envelope, so SSB power is given as peak envelope power, P E P: the power at the highest peaks. The most likely power level for initial MF-HF communications is 150 watts P E P. Use only the power you need: extra power just adds interference for other stations. Raise it only if the other station has trouble copying. Of the other exam choices, 25 and 50 watts may not get through at working distances, and 600 watts is far more than a first call needs.

params.title: Making SITOR (NBDP) with the SSB transmitter

blocks.label: SSB transmitter
blocks.note: Moves the tones up to RF

onScreen: 1700 Hz from the carrier: a 170 Hz shift
scenes.narration: Telex goes through the same transmitter. SITOR, or NBDP, is made the same way as DSC. The most common method on shipboard GMDSS equipment is to feed audio tones into the SSB transmitter. The telex unit turns each bit into one of the 2 tones, and the SSB transmitter moves them up into its upper sideband. On the air, that's 2 alternating sidebands of 1615 hertz and 1785 hertz, offset from the carrier frequency by 1700 hertz: 1700 plus or minus 85 hertz, a 170 hertz shift. That's emission J2B, and on the air it looks just like F1B. The trap answers shift the carrier itself, or use other tones, such as 1500 and 2300 hertz around 1900.

params.title: Power meter on a 60 W PEP set: J3E
rows: Flickers up to 60 W, never steady

onScreen: Speech: flickers up to 60 W, not above
scenes.narration: On to transmitter faults, where your best tool is the RF power meter, which shows how much power is going to the antenna. Take an SSB transmitter rated at 60 watts P E P, working properly in J3E. Key it, meaning switch it to transmit, without speaking: there's no carrier, so no power output is indicated. Speak, and the meter flickers widely with your voice peaks, up to but not above 60 watts. It never holds steady. So no indication of power output when speaking into the microphone is a symptom of malfunction in a 2182 kilohertz SSB radiotelephone. The trap answer for that question is the range check from the start: missing a shore station 600 nautical miles away by day is normal.

params.title: The same meter in SITOR (NBDP) ARQ

badges.label: 3-character block
badges.note: Meter jumps to the 60 W reading

scenes.narration: Switch the same 60 watt set to SITOR, or NBDP, in ARQ. Remember the rhythm: a 210 millisecond block of 3 characters, then a pause to listen for the acknowledgement. While sending, the transmitter puts out full power; while listening, it puts out nothing. So in proper operation, the power meter can be seen fluctuating regularly from 0 to the 60 watt reading. That steady, regular swing is what healthy ARQ looks like.

onScreen: Most likely: failed 500 Hz I.F. filter
Flag: '1615 kHz audio oscillator' means 1615 Hz
scenes.narration: Next symptom: the MF-HF transceiver works properly on voice, but not on SITOR, or NBDP. Use the shared-or-single logic. Working voice proves the exciter, the synthesizer and the power amplifier are fine. NBDP depends on 2 parts voice never uses. One is the tone oscillator that makes the 1615 and 1785 hertz tones. The other is the 500 hertz I.F. filter: in a transceiver, receive and transmit often share the I.F. filters, and this narrow one serves only NBDP. On one exam question, the failed 500 hertz I.F. filter is the most likely source of the problem. A flag note: another question, with the same symptom, keys 'the 1615 kilohertz audio oscillator is not working'. It means the 1615 hertz tone oscillator: without that tone, the transmitter can't form the NBDP signal, so pick that choice.

params.title: F1B on bigger sets: ARQ versus FEC

badges.label: 150 W set, F1B ARQ
badges.note: 210 ms blocks and pauses, repeating every 450 ms

badges.label: Trap: the S meter
badges.note: It reads incoming signals, not transmitted power

onScreen: ARQ, 150 W set: fluctuates 0 to 150 W
FEC, 250 W set: constant 225 to 250 W
Not the S meter: it reads received signals
scenes.narration: Back to the power meter, now on bigger transmitters in F1B, the radio telex emission. A 150 watt MF-HF transmitter working properly in F1B ARQ mode shows an output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts: the 210 millisecond blocks and listening pauses, repeating every 450 milliseconds. FEC is different. It never waits for a reply, so it sends continuously. And an FSK signal has a constant envelope: it shifts frequency, never strength. So a 250 watt transmitter working properly in F1B FEC mode shows constant output between 225 and 250 watts, steady and close to its rating. Trap answers use the S meter, the receiver's Signal meter, which reads incoming signals, not transmitted power, or say output appears only while keys are typed.

params.title: Proper or improper? F1B power readings

scenes.narration: Put the readings side by side, because the exam likes to swap the modes. A swing from 0 to 150 watts is proper in ARQ. Constant output near full power is proper in FEC: 225 to 250 watts on a 250 watt set, or 125 to 150 watts on a 150 watt set. But in F1B FEC mode, an output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts on a 150 watt transmitter indicates improper operation. That swing is normal only for ARQ. In FEC, it means something is cutting the output in and out.

Another reading the exam offers for that 150 watt FEC set: an SWR meter showing 125 watts forward and 5 watts reflected. Forward power travels up to the antenna; reflected power bounces back. Is that acceptable? First find the reflection coefficient, gamma, which says how much of the wave bounces back. Power goes with the square of a wave's size, so gamma is the square root of reflected over forward power: the square root of 5 over 125. 5 over 125 is 1 twenty-fifth, and its square root is 1 fifth, or 0.2. Then SWR is 1 plus gamma, over 1 minus gamma: 1.2 over 0.8, which is 1.5 to 1. That's acceptable, so this reading is not a sign of improper operation.

params.title: Very low RF output: high SWR
items: High SWR in the antenna system: much of the power bounces back
The protection circuit cuts power to save the power amplifier: very low RF output
Dummy load: a matched 50 Ω termination, so full output

onScreen: Protection cuts power: very low RF output
scenes.narration: What if the output is too low? In F1B FEC mode, very low RF output can be caused by a high standing wave ratio in the antenna system. So much power bounces back that the transmitter's protection circuit cuts the power to save the power amplifier. A dummy load won't do that. It's a matched 50 ohm termination, a load that ends the line with exactly 50 ohms, so the transmitter gives full output into it.

onScreen: Power supply: DC for the transmitter
Crowbar: shorts the supply if the voltage surges
scenes.narration: And zero output? Start at the power supply. It feeds the transmitter DC, direct current, the steady one-way kind a battery gives. A crowbar circuit guards against a fault in the supply itself. If the supply voltage starts rising out of control, the crowbar shorts the supply output, like a crowbar thrown across the terminals, blowing a fuse or shutting the supply down. That protects the transmitter from the surge. So activation of a crowbar circuit, to prevent an unregulated voltage increase, shuts off DC power to the transmitter, and RF output drops to 0.

params.title: Valid ways to find an F1B FEC fault
rows: Power supply checks with a DVM
Not valid: F1B just shifts 170 Hz

onScreen: Spectrum analyzer deviation test: not valid
scenes.narration: Last, the tools. Which troubleshooting methods are valid for an F1B FEC transmitter? Visual inspection is: check the control settings and look for damage or overheating. So is power supply testing with a DVM, a digital voltmeter, to confirm each voltage is within limits. So are input and output checks with a 10 to 1 oscilloscope probe. An oscilloscope draws a signal's shape on a screen, and the probe barely disturbs the circuit, so you can trace the signal stage by stage to find where it degrades. The one that's not valid is modulation testing with an RF spectrum analyzer to measure frequency deviation. A spectrum analyzer shows signals by frequency, and deviation is how far an FM voice signal swings. F1B just shifts between 2 fixed frequencies 170 hertz apart, so there's no swing to measure.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: J3E: 2.8 kHz on 3.0 kHz channels · NBDP: 300 Hz on 500 Hz, tones 1615 / 1785 Hz
DSC: 200-bit dot pattern, 10-bit code, 400 ms · ARQ: 3-character blocks · FEC: sent twice
BFO restores the carrier · R.I.T. moves receive only · faults: shared part or single path
150 W PEP to start · power meter: ARQ swings 0 to full, FEC holds steady

onScreen: 200 bits, 10-bit code, 400 ms · ARQ blocks, FEC twice
BFO, R.I.T., shared part or single path
150 W PEP · ARQ swings, FEC steady
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up with 5 things to carry away. First, the 6 DSC frequencies: 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kilohertz, with transmitters held within 10 hertz. Second, voice takes 2.8 kilohertz on 3.0 kilohertz channels, and NBDP 300 hertz on 500 hertz channels, using tones of 1615 and 1785 hertz. Third, a DSC call starts with a 200 bit dot pattern, uses a 10 bit code, and repeats each character 400 milliseconds later, while SITOR's ARQ sends 3-character blocks and FEC sends everything twice. Fourth, the BFO restores the SSB carrier, R.I.T. moves only the receive frequency, and to find a fault, ask whether everything fails or just one mode. Fifth, start contacts at 150 watts P E P, and on the power meter, ARQ swings from 0 to full power while FEC holds steady.
